Deep learning models have achieved impressive success across a wide range of tasks, yet they can behave unpredictably when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) data that differ significantly from the training distribution, making high-confidence but incorrect predictions. OOD detection seeks to identify such inputs and is critical for reliable deployment in open-world scenarios, including safety-critical applications and scientific discovery tasks. The challenge becomes even more pronounced for graph-structured data, because of their non-Euclidean nature and complex topological structures.

Recent advances in graph-level OOD detection fall broadly into two categories. End-to-end methods train OOD-specific graph neural networks (GNNs) from scratch using only unlabeled in-distribution (ID) data; they typically rely on unsupervised objectives such as graph contrastive learning to extract discriminative representations that can separate ID and OOD samples during inference. Post-hoc methods instead start from well-trained GNNs and fine-tune OOD detectors that refine the predictions or representations at inference time. Among them, a recent test-time method, GOODAT, directly optimizes a learnable graph masker on the test samples without altering the pre-trained model. This test-time setting with data-centric modification is more practical, because it removes the dependency on labeled training data and on model retraining.

The test-time problem can be stated as follows. A GNN has been pre-trained on graphs from an unlabeled ID dataset. At test time it faces unlabeled graphs that mix held-out ID graphs, disjoint from the pre-training graphs, with graphs drawn from a different, OOD distribution. The goal is a detector that assigns each test graph a score, a higher score meaning a greater probability that the graph comes from the OOD distribution, using only the pre-trained model and the test graphs: the parameters of the pre-trained model are not modified, and neither the training data nor any ground-truth label is used.

Despite the progress of this data-centric paradigm, a less-explored challenge persists. A pre-trained model can effectively extract information from ID data, but when it infers on both ID and OOD test graphs it lacks ground-truth information indicative of the underlying distribution, information that is often embedded within the graph structure. Test graphs typically comprise distinctive components, whose capture could intuitively differentiate OOD samples from ID graphs, together with irrelevant structural elements. The pervasive presence of similar irrelevant structural elements in ID and OOD graphs, a structural redundancy that induces semantic shifts, hinders current methods from accurately capturing and distinguishing the essential structures of ID and OOD data. The existing test-time method tries to address this concern by using graph maskers to identify subgraphs in the test data that are similar to those in the ID training graphs, but it fundamentally relies on learnable graph augmentations, which can inadvertently alter the semantic information of substructures or lead to information loss, thereby compromising the reliability of OOD detection.

This raises the following questions. How can a well-trained GNN, left unchanged, be endowed at test time with the ability to capture the essential, distinctive structural information of test graphs while discarding irrelevant structural redundancy, without altering the semantics of their substructures? How can what is essential for telling ID from OOD graphs be separated from what is redundant in a principled and tractable way, when neither ground-truth labels nor OOD examples are available? And can such a test-time detector yield more reliable OOD scores than existing end-to-end and post-hoc approaches while remaining practical in computational cost?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Graph Signal Processing (GSP) for Essential Structure Extraction
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the application of GSP primitives, such as graph filtering and graph wavelets, to extract essential structural information from test graphs without altering the semantics of their substructures. We will compare the effectiveness of different GSP-based methods on separating OOD graphs from ID graphs on three real-world datasets: D3R (molecular property prediction), PDB (protein function classification), and Stanford Large Network Dataset Collection (social network analysis). Specifically, we will use the following settings: (1) use a pre-trained GNN as a feature extractor, apply GSP primitives to the output features, and train a simple classifier to separate OOD graphs from ID graphs; and (2) apply GSP primitives directly to the adjacency matrices of test graphs and use a similarity metric (e.g., cosine similarity) to compare the resulting graph signals.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the GOODAT method on the same datasets, and ablate on different GSP primitives and similarity metrics.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect GSP-based methods to outperform the GOODAT method on OOD detection tasks, particularly when the essential structural information is highly correlated with the task-relevant features. However, the performance may degrade when the structural redundancy is severe, and the GSP primitives fail to capture the essential information effectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Homotopy-based Regularization for Irrelevant Structural Redundancy Elimination
PROPOSAL: This experiment develops a novel regularization technique, inspired by homotopy theory, to eliminate irrelevant structural redundancy from test graphs while preserving essential structural information. The regularization term encourages the GNN to learn a transformation that maps ID graphs to the target manifold (i.e., the set of ID graphs) and OOD graphs to the virtual manifold (i.e., an abstract space where OOD graphs reside). The homotopy-based regularization is combined with GSP primitives to refine the transformation, ensuring that essential structural information is preserved. We will evaluate the effectiveness of this approach on the three benchmark datasets using a settings similar to the previous experiment.
CONTROLS: Compare the regularization technique with GSP-based methods and the GOODAT method, and ablate on different homotopy-based regularizers and GSP primitives.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the homotopy-based regularization to improve the OOD detection accuracy by effectively eliminating irrelevant structural redundancy, but its performance may degrade when the virtual manifold is highly non-linear and the homotopy-based regularization fails to capture the underlying structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable Structure Learning for Pre-trained GNNs
PROPOSAL: This theoretical result proves that a pre-trained GNN can be endowed with the ability to capture the essential structural information of test graphs through transferable structure learning. We will derive a theoretical framework that allows a pre-trained GNN to adaptively learn a new structure-aware feature extractor from the test data, which focuses on extracting task-relevant features from the graph structure. The transferable structure learning framework will be evaluated on its ability to improve OOD detection accuracy on three synthetic datasets with varying levels of structural redundancy and essential information.
CONTROLS: Compare the theoretical framework with existing structure learning methods and evaluate its robustness to different levels of structural redundancy.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the transferable structure learning framework to improve the OOD detection accuracy by effectively capturing the essential structural information, but its performance may degrade when the pre-trained GNN lacks sufficient representational power or when the test data is highly non-stationary.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Transferable Structure Learning for Pre-trained GNNs
PROPOSAL: This theoretical result is revised to provide a more detailed proof of the transferable structure learning framework. We will derive a closed-form solution for the structure-aware feature extractor by leveraging the properties of graph signal processing and the pre-trained GNN's representational capacity. The revised framework will be evaluated on its ability to reduce the computational cost of transferable structure learning while maintaining its accuracy on synthetic datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised framework with the original theory and evaluate its empirical performance on synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised framework to improve the efficiency of transferable structure learning without compromising its accuracy, but its performance may degrade when the pre-trained GNN is not well-suited for the task at hand.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Exploring Graph Signal Processing (GSP) for Essential Structure Extraction
PROPOSAL: This experiment is revised to incorporate domain-specific graph spectral features (DSGSF) into the GSP pipeline. We will use DSGSF to preprocess the graph signals before applying GSP primitives, and then evaluate the effectiveness of the revised pipeline on the three real-world datasets. Specifically, we will use a pre-trained GNN as a feature extractor, apply DSGSF to the output features, and then apply GSP primitives to the preprocessed features.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the original GSP method and with GOODAT on the same datasets, and ablate on different DSGSF methods and GSP pipelines.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised pipeline with DSGSF to improve the OOD detection accuracy by effectively capturing domain-specific structural features, but its performance may degrade when the DSGSF fails to generalize across domains or when the GSP pipeline is oversensitive to the preprocessed features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph Data Augmentation for Enhanced OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the effect of graph data augmentation on OOD detection using a pre-trained GNN. We will generate new graphs by applying different graph augmentation techniques (e.g., graph convolutional network (GCN)-based augmentations, random node/edge removal, and graph Fourier transform-based augmentations) to the test graphs, and then evaluate the impact of these augmentations on OOD detection accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the GOODAT method and ablate on different augmentation techniques and their combinations.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect graph data augmentation to improve the OOD detection accuracy by increasing the diversity of the input data, but its performance may degrade when the augmentation techniques fail to capture the essential structural information or when the pre-trained GNN is oversensitive to the augmented data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-task Learning for Robust OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the effectiveness of multi-task learning for robust OOD detection using a pre-trained GNN. We will train the GNN on both the OOD detection task and a related downstream task (e.g., node classification or graph regression), and evaluate the impact of multi-task learning on OOD detection accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the GOODAT method and ablate on different downstream tasks and hyperparameters.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect multi-task learning to improve the OOD detection accuracy by learning robust representation that generalizes well across different tasks, but its performance may degrade when the downstream task is not well-aligned with the OOD detection task or when the pre-trained GNN is not well-suited for multi-task learning.

TITLE: Exploring Graph Signal Processing (GSP) for Essential Structure Extraction
PROPOSAL: This experiment is revised to incorporate transfer learning from a pre-trained GNN into the GSP pipeline. We will use a pre-trained GNN as a feature extractor, apply GSP primitives to the output features, and then fine-tune the pre-trained GNN on in-distribution data to adapt to the GSP features. This will allow us to leverage the learned features from the pre-trained GNN while adapting them to the GSP features.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the original GSP method, the GOODAT method, and ablate on different pre-trained GNNs and hyperparameters.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised pipeline to improve the OOD detection accuracy by leveraging the knowledge from the pre-trained GNN and adapting it to the GSP features, but its performance may degrade when the pre-trained GNN is not well-suited for the task or when the fine-tuning process overfits the data.

TITLE: Hybrid Approach for Enhanced OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: This experiment combines the strengths of multiple approaches by proposing a hybrid framework that integrates the GSP pipeline, transferable structure learning, and multi-task learning. We will use a pre-trained GNN as a feature extractor, apply GSP primitives to the output features, and then fine-tune the pre-trained GNN on in-distribution data to adapt to the GSP features. Additionally, we will train the GNN on both the OOD detection task and a related downstream task, and use a weighted ensemble to combine the predictions from the different components.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the state-of-the-art methods, GOODAT, and ablate on different component combinations and hyperparameters.
COST: 160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the hybrid approach to outperform the individual components and state-of-the-art methods by leveraging their strengths and reducing their weaknesses, but its performance may degrade when the different components conflict with each other or when the hyperparameter tuning process fails to find the optimal combination.

TITLE: Ablation Study and Model Selection for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: This experiment conducts an ablation study on the individual components of the hybrid approach and model selection to identify the most effective architecture and hyperparameter settings for OOD detection. We will conduct extensive experiments on the three real-world datasets and evaluate the performance of different architectures and hyperparameter settings.
CONTROLS: Compare the results with the state-of-the-art methods, GOODAT, and ablate on different architectures and hyperparameter settings.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the ablation study and model selection to provide valuable insights into the most effective architecture and hyperparameter settings for OOD detection and help identify areas for future improvement.

Modern generative paradigms, including diffusion, flow matching and consistency models, have achieved state-of-the-art performance and form the backbone of leading image and video generation systems, including large multi-modal generative models. Despite their success, they share a critical drawback: both training and sampling demand substantial computational resources. Multi-step frameworks such as diffusion and flow matching produce a sample by iteratively integrating a probability-flow ordinary differential equation, typically requiring 40 to 100 network function evaluations (NFEs). The problem is magnified for large-scale models, for which efficient sampling is paramount: the continuous, long-term cost of inference often surpasses the one-time training cost, directly affecting economic viability and practical deployment. For example, the largest open multi-modal image generators (about 20B parameters) typically need about 100 NFEs, i.e. roughly 40 seconds on a single A100 GPU for one 1024×1024 image.

Numerous efforts aim to accelerate generative inference by reducing the number of sampling steps. Early single-step generators such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) often suffered from unstable training dynamics. To accelerate multi-step diffusion models, various distillation techniques have been introduced. They range from student-teacher methods, in which a student learns to reproduce a frozen teacher's sampling trajectory in fewer steps (e.g., progressive distillation, which requires an iterative distillation procedure), to distribution matching distillation (e.g., DMD and DMD2), which uses adversarial-style training with auxiliary networks to align the generator's output distribution directly with the data distribution. In parallel, consistency models and their variants (e.g., LCM and PCM), as well as related shortcut and MeanFlow objectives, have been designed explicitly for high-quality generation in very few steps, and recent work shows that multi-step and few-step models can be cast as instances of a single unified any-step training objective.

Despite this progress, existing few-step methods face a difficult trade-off between simplicity, efficiency and quality. (a) Complexity and instability: adversarial approaches, such as GANs, DMD-style distribution matching and hybrid frameworks that combine teacher guidance with adversarial signals (e.g., SANA-Sprint), require auxiliary trained networks (discriminators or fake-sample score networks) and/or frozen teacher models; distribution matching methods typically keep separate copies of a generator, a real-score model and a fake-score model. This introduces training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters, and it increases architectural complexity and GPU memory overhead. For ultra-large models, the added complexity often translates into out-of-memory failures or brittle training dynamics, so few-step approaches have rarely been applied to models beyond about 3B parameters, and the only open-source few-step model released for a large model was obtained by distribution matching distillation with its GAN loss removed, an indirect sign of the high cost of adversarial losses at scale. (b) Performance degradation: methods trained without adversarial guidance, such as consistency models, often show a sharp decline in quality at very low NFEs (fewer than 4), and within the unified any-step view, current few-step methods struggle to reach high-quality one-step generation without resorting to a GAN-style loss.

The open problem is therefore how to train a generator that produces high-quality images in a single function evaluation, or very few, without discriminators, auxiliary score networks or frozen teacher models, so that training remains simple, stable and memory-efficient enough to scale to full-parameter training of the largest (10B to 20B parameters) text-to-image and multi-modal generators, without sacrificing the quality obtained by multi-step sampling.

TITLE: Simplified Unified Any-Step Training (SUAST) Objective
PROPOSAL: Derive and experimentally evaluate the effectiveness of a simplified unified any-step training (SUAST) objective for few-step generative models, combining ideas from consistency-based and adversarial training objectives in a straightforward and computationally efficient manner. Specifically, define the SUAST objective using a form that averages a consistency loss with a predictive loss derived from the generative model's own output distribution (e.g., KL divergence or cross-entropy), without the need for auxilaries networks, discriminators, or frozen teacher models.
CONTROLS: Experiment on the same architectures and settings as consistency-based few-step models (e.g., LCM) while repurposing their consistency loss as the objective, and train with and without a KL constraint between the generator's output and a fixed distribution (e.g., Gaussian or uniform) to gauge the role of latent exploration in SUAST, as part of the same evaluation.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Rivaling the performance of current few-step models, including consistency-based LCM and PCM, with comparable or smaller computing resources. SUAST could excel in certain regimes where a fixed or loosely-constrained generator distribution benefits generation. Yet debugging and interpretable explanations for SUAST might be harder due to the lack of explicit adversarial signals.

TITLE: Anchor Loss for Simplified Unified Any-Step Training (SUAST)
PROPOSAL: Introduce an Anchor Loss component to the SUAST objective to help guide the generator's output distribution towards a well-defined anchor (e.g., a simple image prior or a snippet-based text representation) during few-step training. This should help stabilize training, improve sample quality, and potentially allow for faster convergence.
CONTROLS: Compare the effect of Anchor Loss on few-step generation quality and convergence speed with baseline SUAST training, and examine how Anchor Loss interacts with different architectures and input distributions in the ULTRA-SUAST-ARGaTAN framework, under the conditions stated above.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: SUAST with Anchor Loss yields consistent improvements in few-step generation quality and stability across diverse architectures and tasks, bolstering its suitability for large-scale applications.

TITLE: Anchor Loss for Simplified Unified Any-Step Training (SUAST)
REVISED PROPOSAL: Modify the Anchor Loss component in the SUAST objective to be adaptive, dynamically adjusting its influence on the generator's output based on the current training dynamics and task requirements. This should enable the Anchor Loss to provide more nuanced guidance throughout training, potentially leading to even better improvements in few-step generation quality and stability.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance of adaptive Anchor Loss with that of the original non-adaptive version, examining the trade-offs between baseline convergence speed, few-step generation quality, and sample diversity. Evaluate the effectiveness of adaptive Anchor Loss across different architectures, input distributions, and tasks.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive Anchor Loss improves upon non-adaptive Anchor Loss, consistently achieving better few-step generation quality, more stable training, and higher sample diversity, while discovering new regimes where it outperforms the baseline SUAST training.

TITLE: Few-Step Latent Matcher for Real-World Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a Few-Step Latent Matcher module to learn a compact, structure-preserving space that captures the essential image features from the real-world text-to-image generation setting, enabling the few-step generator to focus on accurately reconstructing these features. This should improve the quality and realism of generated images while reducing computational demands.
CONTROLS: Compare the Few-Step Latent Matcher with state-of-the-art few-step and multi-step text-to-image generation models on real-world benchmarks, investigating the impact of architecture, input distribution, and task specifics on matcher performance.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The Few-Step Latent Matcher consistently enhances the quality and realism of generated images, narrowing the gap with multi-step models while providing the efficiency benefits of few-step generation, and demonstrating its versatility across diverse architectures, input distributions, and tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Few-Step Latent Matcher for Real-World Text-to-Image Generation
REVISED PROPOSAL: Integrate the Few-Step Latent Matcher module with the Anchor Loss component in the SUAST objective to create a hybrid approach that fuels the few-step generator's ability to capture and reconstruct essential image features from the real-world text-to-image generation setting. This should further enhance the quality and realism of generated images, potentially enabling few-step generation to outperform multi-step methods in total computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the hybrid approach on real-world benchmarks, comparing it with the anchor-only SUAST, SUAST with adaptive Anchor Loss, and Few-Step Latent Matcher in isolation, to quantify the synergy between these components and the incremental benefits of the hybrid method, in the main experimental setting.
COST: 450 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hybrid approach breaks the state-of-the-art for few-step text-to-image generation, efficiently generating high-quality and realistic images while requiring significantly fewer computational resources than multi-step methods. However, debugging the hybrid method may be more challenging due to its increased complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Few-Step Image Editing with SUAST++
PROPOSAL: Develop a new variant of the SUAST objective, dubbed SUAST++, that specifically targets efficient few-step image editing tasks by incorporating additional terms that encourage spatial coherence, smoothness, and photorealism in edited images. This will be achieved through a combination of novel losses and regularization techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of SUAST++ with SUAST and existing few-step image editing models on various benchmark datasets for image editing, focusing on both efficiency and quality metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and in-painting accuracy.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: SUAST++ achieves state-of-the-art results for few-step image editing tasks, demonstrating better balance between efficiency and quality compared to existing methods. It will be particularly efficient on very large datasets, making it a novel and impactful contribution to the field.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Few-Step Image Editing with SUAST++ and Latent Matching
REVISED PROPOSAL: Integrate the Few-Step Latent Matcher module with the SUAST++ objective for efficient few-step image editing, aiming to further enhance the spatial coherence, smoothness, and photorealism of edited images. This will involve a multi-stage editing framework that leverages the latent matcher to pre-process the image and SUAST++ to refine the edited result.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the integrated framework on benchmark datasets for image editing, comparing it with SUAST++, SUAST++, and Latent Matcher in isolation, as well as with state-of-the-art few-step image editing models.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The integrated framework significantly outperforms existing methods for few-step image editing tasks, achieving superior quality and efficiency results due to the synergistic combination of SUAST++ and Latent Matcher, and showcasing its potential for practical applications in image and video editing.

TITLE: Experimental Evaluation on Real-World Text-to-Image Generation
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive experimental evaluation of the proposed methods (SUAST, ULTRA-SUAST-ARGaTAN, Anchor Loss, Few-Step Latent Matcher, and SUAST++) on real-world text-to-image generation benchmarks, using the COCO and Flickr30K datasets, and investigating their performance on metrics including FID, inception score, and visual coherence.

PREDICTION: The comprehensive evaluation provides a clear ranking of the proposed methods, highlighting their relative strengths on different metrics and datasets, and sheds light on the underlying factors contributing to their performance differences, ultimately advancing the state-of-the-art in text-to-image generation and illuminating future research directions.

Multimodal learning has become a cornerstone of many real-world applications, such as autonomous perception, medical diagnosis, and human-computer interaction. By integrating information from multiple sources, such as vision, audio, and text, multimodal systems aim to improve performance and generalization. However, multimodal data often exhibit a significant imbalance between modalities due to noise, lack of information, or sensor heterogeneity, so that a dominant modality may overshadow the others and hinder the learning of weak modalities. Unimodal prediction accuracy is widely used to detect modality imbalance; it is a simple and effective metric, but it is inherently sensitive to noise and perturbations. This vulnerability often leads to fragile performance in practice and limits the reliability of accuracy-based definitions of strong and weak modalities in real-world deployments.

Modality imbalance arises in early, intermediate, and late fusion alike. Late fusion, also known as decision-level fusion, combines the outputs (logits) of modality-specific models, either with equal weights (static late fusion) or with weights that vary across samples (dynamic late fusion). It remains one of the most widely adopted paradigms because of its modular design, interpretability, and strong compatibility with unimodal pre-trained models. Yet, lacking feature-level compensation or cross-modal interaction, late fusion tends to amplify the influence of strong modalities while weakening the role of lower-quality ones, so that predictions from disadvantaged modalities often carry little weight or even introduce noise into the final decision. A large body of work has attempted to alleviate this imbalance by enhancing the predictive performance of weak modalities, for example by aggregating independently trained modality-specific classifiers, confidence-based weighting, modality dropout or gating, adaptive ensembling, or knowledge distillation from dominant modalities.

While effective in certain scenarios, these methods often implicitly aim to align weak modalities with dominant ones in terms of prediction accuracy, attempting to bring them closer to their stronger counterparts. Such over-alignment raises several concerns: (1) it may suppress the distinct and complementary information encoded in weak modalities, causing modality-specific information loss; (2) it risks error propagation, as the dominant modality's errors are amplified when weak modalities follow them blindly; and (3) through excessive conformity, weak modalities may lose the predictive advantages they originally held on some samples.

Robustness makes the issue more pressing. Multimodal cooperation is inherently sensitive to perturbations such as data noise, label noise, and incomplete modalities, because modalities are heterogeneous and vary in reliability in real-world conditions. Prior studies have highlighted that the robustness of a multimodal system can be bottlenecked by a single weak modality, revealing a strong link between modality imbalance and overall system reliability. Existing work addresses robustness by incorporating uncertainty modeling, designing robustness-aware fusion strategies, quantifying multimodal robustness with dedicated evaluation metrics, or connecting it with generalization error bounds. However, most of these approaches emphasize prediction-consistency modeling and pay little attention to the instability of the decision space, that is, a model's high sensitivity to input perturbations near the decision boundary, where even minor changes can cause large shifts in prediction; they also tend to require more complex architectures with limited generalizability across tasks with different class granularity.

This raises several questions. How can a dominant modality help a weak modality within a decision-level fusion system without forcing it to conform, so that the weak modality keeps its unique, complementary information and does not inherit the dominant modality's errors? Given that judging modality strength by unimodal accuracy or confidence is itself fragile under noise, how can one reliably determine which modality is dominant and which is weak? How do the predictions of the individual modalities determine the robustness of the fused decision to input perturbations, and can a remedy for modality imbalance come with a theoretical guarantee on that robustness? Finally, can such a remedy both narrow the performance gap between modalities and make the fused prediction more reliable under noisy and imbalanced conditions?

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Adaptive Confidence Weighting for Late Fusion with Guaranteed Robustness
PROPOSAL: We explore an adaptive confidence weighting method that dynamically adjusts the contribution of modality-specific classifiers based on their expected information gain, without relying on unimodal accuracy or confidence scores. This is achieved by modeling the prediction uncertainty of each modality using Bayesian neural networks, and then leveraging a regret-minimizing algorithm to compute the optimal confidence weights for late fusion. The robustness of the fused decision to input perturbations is ensured through a theoretically grounded bound on the maximum perturbation tolerance, derived using tools from differential privacy and robust aggregation.
CONTROLS: Compare with static confidence weighting, equal weighting, and decision tree-based confidence weighting; evaluate on synthetic vs. real-world datasets with varying levels of noise and imbalance.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: We expect a 10-20% improvement in accuracy and robustness of the fused decision compared to baselines, with significant gains in scenarios with severe modality imbalance and noise; however, we may encounter difficulties in scaling the regret-minimizing algorithm to large datasets.

PROPOSAL: Inspired by the concept of Hedge algorithms for quantifying risk in game theory, we propose HedgeClustering, a novel framework that clusters modalities based on their adverse cavitation boundaries under a novel, adversary-driven loss clustering method. HedgeClustering incorporates a new form of modal-layered loss regularization to ensure low risk (i.e., high robustness) and prohibit distortion of the robust feature space in decision-level fusion. By implicitly grouping sources of information with high risk into clusters and technically safe ones as centres, practical noise abatement and intra modal variation elimination are naturally achieved.

Inverse problems arise in many domains, including computer vision, protein science, medical imaging and scientific computing. The goal is to reconstruct an unknown signal x ∈ R^n from noisy measurements y ∈ R^m, with y = A(x) + η, where A is a known forward operator and η is additive measurement noise. Diffusion models have recently shown powerful capabilities in modeling complex data distributions, and they provide a powerful class of priors for high-dimensional data, such as natural images, when solving inverse problems.

Methods for solving inverse problems fall broadly into two families. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference seeks the single most probable x: it delivers fast optimization, but struggles with high noise and multimodal posteriors and easily converges to local minima. The Bayesian alternative samples from the posterior p(x|y) ∝ p(x) p(y|x) to generate plausible reconstructions, quantify uncertainty and handle multimodality. Both critically depend on a powerful prior, such as a pretrained diffusion model, that encodes the complex statistical structure of the data.

Although diffusion-based solvers have shown remarkable success across diverse inverse problems, current methods suffer from three complementary limitations. (1) Iterative guidance methods, such as DPS, DDRM, DDNM, ΠGDM and TMPD, try to sample the intermediate posteriors p(x_t|y) along the reverse diffusion, which requires the intractable likelihood p(y|x_t) at every intermediate timestep. They approximate it, for example through Tweedie's formula, and apply likelihood-gradient corrections directly to the intermediate states. Because such gradients generally contain components orthogonal to the data manifold, these corrections systematically push the intermediate states off the learned manifold and violate the training-time noise conditioning of the denoiser, leading to failed reconstructions such as accumulated artifacts; even second-order corrections of the guidance trajectory still modify intermediate states and risk drifting off the manifold. (2) Stochastic MAP methods that optimize in image space, such as ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM and DIIP, can match the measurements well with very sharp details, but they require carefully tuned hyperparameters to avoid overfitting to noise, which limits their effectiveness when the noise is high or unknown. Some of them are formulated as posterior samplers yet use a heuristic measurement-noise level much smaller than the true one to strengthen measurement consistency, which makes them effectively MAP-like and equally sensitive to noise. (3) Deterministic MAP methods that optimize over the diffusion model's input noise, such as DMPlug, remove randomness but are sensitive to measurement noise and, lacking posterior exploration, often get stuck in a single mode, especially in severely ill-posed problems such as phase retrieval. Early stopping can limit noise overfitting, but its criterion is task- and noise-dependent, and at high noise levels the optimizer often becomes trapped in a local mode anyway. In short, enforcing data consistency in the middle of the diffusion process can break adherence to the prior, while optimizing only for fidelity leads to overfitting or mode collapse.

These failure modes point to two requirements. A solver should maintain manifold feasibility: the states it feeds to the pretrained denoiser should remain close to the high-probability manifold of the corresponding noise level, so that the final reconstruction lies on the learned data manifold. At the same time, it should explore the posterior well enough to escape spurious local modes, rather than collapsing onto the mode nearest to its initialization.

A further practical difficulty is that the level, and even the type, of measurement noise is often unknown and may not be Gaussian, which makes the likelihood term itself intractable. Existing methods handle this with tunable hyperparameters that control the strength of the likelihood term, or with task-specific early-stopping criteria, typically tuned for one particular type and level of noise; they must therefore be re-tuned for each task, dataset and noise level, which is impractical when the noise is unknown.

This raises the following questions. How can a pretrained diffusion prior be used to sample from the posterior of an inverse problem without approximating intractable intermediate likelihoods and without ever feeding off-manifold states to the denoiser? How can such a sampler explore the solution space well enough to avoid spurious local modes in severely ill-posed, multimodal problems, so that its reconstructions do not depend on the initialization? Can it be robust to measurement noise, in the sense that its reconstructions do not overfit the noise, without hand-tuned regularization weights or early stopping? And can it handle measurement noise of unknown level and type with a single fixed set of hyperparameters across tasks, datasets and noise levels, at a computational cost that remains practical?

Large language models can be knowledge edited, that is, updated to incorporate new or corrected facts without retraining from scratch. This capability is crucial for keeping models up to date with evolving information and for correcting errors on the fly. Large vision-language models (LVLMs), which combine textual and visual understanding, make knowledge editing even more challenging: they encode factual knowledge in both their textual and their visual pathways, and they require mechanisms that update the knowledge of both modalities consistently. Efficiently editing LVLMs is crucial for real-world applications, such as swiftly correcting critical visual recognition errors (e.g., a model misidentifying Donald Trump as Boris Johnson). However, research on multimodal knowledge editing remains scarce compared with the extensive studies on text-only language models.

Existing benchmarks for LVLM knowledge editing are limited in scope. They typically focus only on visual knowledge updates, such as changing the identity that an image is recognized as, and overlook scenarios in which textual facts about an entity (e.g., its attributes, roles or affiliations) must also be updated. Furthermore, they do not evaluate continual editing, in which multiple knowledge updates are performed sequentially, nor do they test a model's ability to reason compositionally over edited facts. This is a critical gap, because real-world knowledge updates often arrive incrementally and involve intertwined visual and textual information: once a model has been corrected about who appears in a photo and, separately, updated with a new fact about that person, a question about the person in the photo can only be answered correctly by combining both edits.

Existing editing approaches face fundamental difficulties in this setting. External-memory editors store edited knowledge outside the model and retrieve relevant information at inference time without modifying model parameters, which makes them suitable for long-term retention. However, they typically transplant text-based retrieval strategies from language models directly, ignoring visual cues that are necessary for matching multimodal queries to the right edits, which can reduce retrieval accuracy. They also face an internalization issue: the model may over-rely on its stale internal knowledge, especially when the retrieved information conflicts with what it has learned, leading to incorrect answers. Conversely, internal-memory editors embed edits directly into model parameters via fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation, viewing the feed-forward network as a key-value memory that stores in-model knowledge. Although beneficial for internalizing edits, these methods typically store visual and textual edits within a unified representation space, risking cross-modal interference and representation collapse; moreover, sequential internal edits suffer from catastrophic forgetting, degrading previously stored knowledge with successive updates.

This raises several questions. How can an LVLM accommodate a continual sequence of interleaved visual and textual edits so that each new edit takes effect while earlier edits are retained, without interference between modalities? How can separately edited visual and textual facts be integrated to answer compositional queries that require both, even when externally retrieved evidence and the model's internal knowledge disagree? And how can editors be evaluated in this continual and compositional setting, which existing benchmarks do not cover?

TITLE: Unified Visual-Textual Memory Update for Large Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel memory architecture that dynamically updates the visual and textual knowledge of an LVLM in a unified yet modality-sensitive manner, using a learnable attention mechanism to selectively integrate new information from both sources. Specifically, we introduce a dual-memory network where the textual memory stores edited textual knowledge and the visual memory stores edited visual knowledge. During each update step, the LVLM attends to relevant visual or textual features and selectively merges the new information into both memories, ensuring that the edited knowledge from both modalities remains consistent.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with traditional external-memory editing strategies, internal-memory editors that embed edits into a unified representation space, and a baseline that fine-tunes the entire LVLM on the edited dataset.

PREDICTION: Our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in continual multimodal knowledge editing and compositionally integrating edited visual and textual facts, demonstrating robustness under sequential updates. Recording dynamic scenes from multiple viewpoints has become increasingly common in everyday life. From concerts and sports events to lectures and birthday parties, people often capture the same moment using different handheld devices. These multi-view recordings present a rich opportunity to reconstruct scenes in 4D, enable bullet-time effects, or enhance the capabilities of existing vision models. However, these videos are typically captured independently, without synchronization or known camera poses, making it difficult to align and fuse them coherently.

The task is the following: given a set of asynchronous videos that capture the same dynamic scene from different viewpoints, estimate a time offset for each video, to be applied to its original out-of-sync clock, so that after correction frames sharing the same clock time correspond to the exact same moment across all videos.

Existing synchronization methods rely on controlled environments, manual annotations, specific patterns such as human pose, audio signals such as flashes or claps, or expensive hardware setups such as time-coded devices, none of which are available in casually captured videos. Human-centric approaches, which use body pose as the synchronization signal, are limited by the accuracy of pose estimation and by the number of people present, and they struggle in scenes without prominent human activity. Audio-based approaches only work in quiet environments and do not carry over to in-the-wild settings where audio is noisy or unavailable. Methods that jointly optimize camera poses and temporal offsets within a learned scene representation are often constrained to specific environments or object types. Geometry-based methods estimate temporal offsets from multi-view geometric constraints, but typically assume static scenes or a fixed viewpoint. Meanwhile, structure-from-motion and learned camera-pose estimators recover camera geometry accurately, yet they rely predominantly on static visual cues and therefore fall short of synchronizing dynamic scenes.

Building a practical and robust synchronization system that works on videos in the wild is challenging. Camera poses are unknown and cameras may move, so the geometric relationship between each pair of cameras must itself be estimated reliably. The moving objects that carry the timing information are not known in advance and are generally small and blurry. Associating points across cameras with significantly different viewpoints is difficult. The offsets to be recovered are continuous, while observations arrive only at discrete frame times. Finally, not all views overlap, so some pairs of cameras may share little spatial or temporal overlap.

This raises several questions. How can a set of casually captured, unposed and unsynchronized videos of the same dynamic scene be aligned in time with high precision, without specialized capture, audio, manual correction, or assumptions about the scene content such as the presence of people? Which visual evidence can reliably reveal the temporal offset between two cameras whose poses are unknown and possibly changing over time? And how can a single, globally consistent offset be recovered for every video when the evidence relating some pairs of views is weak, ambiguous or missing? Answering these questions would open the door to scalable, unconstrained multi-view 4D scene understanding and to downstream tasks, such as 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes, that depend on synchronized input.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit compelling cross-modal perception and reasoning capabilities on image-text data and have become the de facto standard for visual question answering (VQA), the task of answering a question based on the visual content of an image. However, standard MLLM architectures are not well suited to perceiving and reasoning about small visual details in high-resolution images. So-called global-view MLLMs downscale every input image to the base resolution of their vision encoder (for some widely used models only 224×224 or 336×336 pixels), which discards information; as a consequence, they perform poorly on fine-grained VQA, i.e., on questions whose answer depends on small visual details. Unlike common VQA settings, in which the question-relevant objects are typically prominent in the image, fine-grained VQA concerns targets that may occupy only a tiny fraction of a large, high-resolution image.

More recent global-local-view MLLMs process a downsampled global view together with local crops extracted from the original, unresized image. This dual-view strategy reduces information loss, but it multiplies the number of visual tokens, and because self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, the computational cost grows rapidly. Moreover, despite having access to fine-grained visual details from all local crops, these models struggle to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question amid the large number of local crop tokens, so their effectiveness on fine-grained VQA still remains limited.

An orthogonal line of work is visual cropping: searching the image for the regions that are relevant to the question and passing only those regions to the MLLM. Existing visual cropping techniques, however, suffer from one or more of three limitations. First, some depend on task-specific fine-tuning: SEAL, for instance, pairs the answering model with a separate visual-search MLLM equipped with additional decoders that is fine-tuned to predict object heatmaps and coordinates, and runs a recursive top-down search, a complex multi-module design that is costly to run. Second, several rely on uninformed, exhaustive search: DC² builds a hierarchical tree of image regions and captions each region with the MLLM, while ZoomEye traverses a hierarchical region tree and scores every visited region with three sequential MLLM forward passes using different prompts, a computation that cannot be simplified or shared across regions, so the cost grows quickly with the depth and breadth of the search. Third, ViCrop avoids hierarchical search by directly computing a question-guided heatmap, but its best-performing variants depend on query-key attention weights and answer gradients, which makes them incompatible with efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention that never explicitly produce attention weights. Simply asking the MLLM where the target is does not solve the problem either: although many MLLMs are fine-tuned to predict bounding boxes, they often fail when prompted directly for the location of small objects, producing hallucinated or imprecise coordinates.

The open problem is therefore how to make an MLLM look at the right part of a high-resolution image. Can the image regions relevant to a fine-grained visual question be localized without task-specific fine-tuning or auxiliary modules, without an uninformed exhaustive search over the image, and in a way that remains compatible with efficient attention implementations? Can such localization benefit both global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, improving their answers to questions about small details while keeping inference cost low, given that MLLM inference is already computationally expensive? And how favorable an accuracy-efficiency trade-off can be reached relative to existing search-based visual cropping methods?

Explaining the prediction of a machine learning model is as important as building the model itself, since it helps determine whether the model can be trusted to give meaningful predictions when deployed in the real world. Such explanations of black-box decisions are all the more important in sensitive applications, such as medicine, finance, and law.

In the quest to explain models, a recent line of research has focused on developing local explanation methods, whose objective is to identify the degree of influence that each feature of a specific data point has on the model prediction. These include explanation vectors, LIME, and Shapley values. When local methods are expressed as additive feature attribution methods, i.e., when the feature influences add up linearly to give the model prediction, game-theoretic results guarantee that Shapley values provide the unique solution to additive feature attribution. For these reasons, Shapley values have emerged as a front-runner among model-agnostic explanation tools. They have also found relevance in other machine learning applications, such as global sensitivity analysis, where they have been used to partition the coefficient of determination in linear regression. More concretely, Shapley values offer a general approach to answering the following question: given a model $f$ trained on data points with $d$ features and evaluated on a test sample $\bm{q} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, how does each feature of $\bm{q}$ locally influence the final model decision $f(\bm{q})$?

Consider a value function $v: 2^{[d]} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $v(S)$ depends on the output of the model on the test sample $\bm{q}$ using only the features in the subset $S$ of $[d] = \{1, \ldots, d\}$. For instance, given a baseline $\bm{q}^{\textup{base}}$, one may define $v(S) = f(\bm{q}^{(S)})$, where $\bm{q}^{(S)}_j = \bm{q}_j$ if $j \in S$ and $\bm{q}^{(S)}_j = \bm{q}^{\textup{base}}_j$ otherwise. The Shapley value of the $j$-th feature is $\phi_j^* = \sum_{S \subseteq [d] \setminus \{j\}} \frac{|S|!(d-|S|-1)!}{d!} (v(S \cup \{j\}) - v(S))$, the aggregate of the marginal contributions of feature $j$ to the model prediction over all subsets $S$ that do not contain $j$. Computing it requires evaluating $v(S)$ on each of the exponentially many subsets of $[d]$, and each evaluation of $v(S)$ is itself costly, with the exact cost depending on how $v(S)$ is defined. This cost can be reduced for certain types of simple models, but an appealing aspect of Shapley values is their potential for model-agnostic explanations; as $d$ increases, an exact solution quickly cannot be computed and estimation techniques are required. Because Shapley values are increasingly used to interpret model behavior, the quality of the estimator is of the utmost importance: an unfaithful explanation may lead to incorrect model interventions, business decisions, or court judgments whenever model assessment is involved.

To make Shapley values computationally tractable for arbitrary models, multiple randomized estimators have been proposed; they aim to approximate the Shapley values while using only a sub-exponential number of value-function evaluations. Perhaps the most popular is KernelSHAP, which is implemented in the widely used SHAP library. KernelSHAP and related estimators rely on the observation that the Shapley values are the solution to a constrained weighted least-squares problem. Let $\bm{Z}$ be the $(2^d-2) \times d$ binary matrix whose row indexed by a nonempty proper subset $S$ of $[d]$ has entry one in column $j$ exactly when $j \in S$, let $\bm{W}$ be the diagonal matrix of kernel weights $k(S) = (d-1)/(\binom{d}{|S|}|S|(d-|S|))$, and let $\bm{v}_S = v(S) - v(\emptyset)$. Then the vector of Shapley values $\bm{\phi}^*$ minimizes $\|\sqrt{\bm{W}}(\bm{Z}\bm{\phi} - \bm{v})\|^2$ over all $\bm{\phi} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying $\bm{1}^\top \bm{\phi} = v([d]) - v(\emptyset)$. Like the definition itself, this regression formulation requires knowing $v(S)$ for every subset of $[d]$. To get around this cost, KernelSHAP randomly subsamples and reweights the rows of the regression problem, sampling the row of subset $S$ with probability proportional to its kernel weight $k(S)$ (a choice motivated by the fact that the least-squares objective can be written as an expectation with respect to this sampling distribution), and then outputs the solution of the much smaller constrained regression problem. Other practical improvements, such as paired sampling and sampling without replacement, are also included in the SHAP library implementation of KernelSHAP.

A large number of subsequent works have built on KernelSHAP. Of particular relevance are unbiased KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, which appear to be the only extensions of KernelSHAP with theoretical convergence guarantees. Unbiased KernelSHAP is an unbiased variant of KernelSHAP for which an asymptotic variance analysis is given; however, it has been observed to underperform the original KernelSHAP in practice. LeverageSHAP is a regression-based estimator that samples the rows of the regression problem according to their statistical leverage scores, and it satisfies strong non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees; numerical experiments suggest that it may outperform KernelSHAP in most settings. By contrast, theoretical bounds for KernelSHAP itself, the most influential and widely used of these estimators, have remained elusive, and the tradeoffs between these existing estimators are not well understood.

Several works have also focused specifically on the challenges of computing Shapley values for high-dimensional data. Many of them use parametric approaches to the computation of Shapley values, such as methods based on latent features or the recently proposed SimSHAP, which require overhead model pretraining; others, such as approaches for data structured on graphs, avoid computing Shapley values in large dimensions by leveraging inductive biases, and methods for large language models have also recently been developed. However, no algorithm at present is tailored to high-dimensional settings while providing provable guarantees on sample efficiency.

This leaves several open questions. Can non-asymptotic sample-complexity guarantees be proved for KernelSHAP and, more broadly, for the family of randomized estimators related to it, including estimators that sample subsets with or without replacement? What would such guarantees reveal about the relative performance of existing estimators such as KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, and about how the choice of sampling distribution affects accuracy? And can estimators that come with provable guarantees be made to scale to high-dimensional inputs?

PROPOSAL: We derive non-asymptotic bounds for KernelSHAP's randomized estimator, specifically in terms of the total number of value-function evaluations needed to achieve a desired level of accuracy. Deep neural networks trained with first-order optimization methods have achieved remarkable empirical success across diverse domains. Despite their widespread adoption, a rigorous theoretical understanding of their optimization dynamics and generalization behavior remains incomplete, particularly for networks with ReLU activations. The difficulty stems from the non-smoothness and non-convexity of the loss landscape induced by ReLU activations and network architectures, which complicate classical analyses. Intriguingly, over-parameterized models often reach zero training error and still generalize well in the absence of explicit regularization, a phenomenon that has spurred substantial theoretical research into its underlying mechanisms.

A prominent line of research analyzes neural network training through the neural tangent kernel (NTK). In the infinite-width limit, the dynamics of gradient descent (GD) can be characterized by functions in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the NTK, and convergence guarantees have been established for both shallow and deep networks: provided the width is sufficiently large, GD converges to a global minimum within a neighborhood of its initialization. In this regime, generalization errors of order $L\sqrt{\mathbf{y}^\top(\mathbf{H}^\infty)^{-1}\mathbf{y}/n}$ have been obtained for networks of depth $L$ trained on $n$ examples, where $\mathbf{H}^\infty$ denotes the NTK Gram matrix over the training data, but only for widths polynomial in $n$, $L$ and $1/\lambda_0$, with $\lambda_0$ the smallest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{H}^\infty$. Requiring $\lambda_0>0$ is a strong assumption, because this eigenvalue tends to zero as the size of the training set grows. A weaker assumption is that the data are separable by the NTK features at initialization with a margin $\gamma$. Under this assumption, a logarithmic width suffices for two-layer ReLU networks, with a risk bound of order $1/(\gamma^2\sqrt{n})$ derived from Rademacher complexity; this width result relies on the 1-homogeneity of two-layer ReLU networks, a property that does not hold for deep networks. Extensions to deep ReLU networks yield bounds that still decay only as $1/\sqrt{n}$ and contain either factors exponential in depth, such as $4^L$, or additional width-dependent terms. A rate of order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ has so far been derived only for two-layer ReLU networks. More generally, uniform-convergence analyses based on Rademacher complexity or covering numbers can lead to vacuous bounds, typically depend exponentially on the depth, and usually yield rates of order $1/\sqrt{n}$.

A complementary line of research relies on algorithmic stability. Building on the observation that the spectral norm of the Hessian of wide networks scales with the width $m$ as $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{m})$, stability analyses have obtained bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(1/(n\gamma^2))$ for shallow networks, which is almost optimal in view of known lower bounds, and have been extended to deep networks with bounds of order $\widetilde{O}(e^{O(L)}/(n\gamma^2))$. These analyses, however, assume smooth activation functions and cannot be applied to non-smooth ReLU networks; for deep networks, they also incur an exponential dependence on depth, both in the bound and in the required width.

In summary, existing results either exhibit the suboptimal $1/\sqrt{n}$ dependence on the sample size, are restricted to shallow networks, require smooth activations, or depend exponentially on the depth $L$. A natural and fundamental question is therefore whether GD on deep ReLU networks can achieve generalization rates comparable to the minimax optimal rates established in the kernel setting, namely the SVM-type rate of order $1/(n\gamma^2)$. Specifically, for fully connected deep ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with the logistic loss on binary classification data that are NTK-separable with margin $\gamma$: Can risk bounds of the optimal order $1/(\gamma^2 n)$ be established? Can the exponential dependence on the depth $L$ be replaced by a polynomial dependence $\mathrm{poly}(L)$? And how much over-parameterization (network width) do such guarantees require?

Human-object interaction (HOI) detection aims to localize humans and objects in an image and to recognize the interactions between them. It provides a fine-grained understanding of human activities, which is crucial for downstream applications such as robotic manipulation, image captioning and autonomous driving. Despite recent progress, HOI detection remains challenging because of the large combinatorial space of human-object pairs and the need for fine-grained visual understanding. Moreover, real-world applications often require recognizing human-object interactions that do not appear in the training set, which leads to the task of zero-shot HOI detection. Conventional HOI detectors fail to generalize to such unseen interactions, and early attempts that disentangle object and verb features for compositional generalization cannot handle unseen objects or unseen verbs.

To address zero-shot HOI detection, recent works exploit vision-language models such as CLIP to transfer semantic knowledge from language to HOI detection. Typically, they use text embeddings of interaction descriptions, e.g., "A person is holding a cup", to construct classifiers for unseen interactions. While effective to some extent, these methods face limitations. First, CLIP features lack the fine-grained representational capacity required to distinguish visually similar interactions, so methods have to incorporate detector features to obtain fine-grained representations of instances. Second, their core mechanism, aligning visual and text features, operates only on categories observed during training, which restricts generalization to unseen interactions.

At the same time, progress in open-vocabulary object detection provides a sufficient solution for localizing unseen objects, so interaction recognition has become the main bottleneck. Yet most existing methods, including two-stage methods, couple interaction recognition with a specific object detector: they rely on detector features or on relations between detected objects to give vision-language features fine-grained representational capacity, and they struggle to balance fine-grained detector features with generalized vision-language features. As a result, interaction recognition and detection cannot be improved independently, and the detector cannot be changed without retraining.

Effective interaction recognition therefore requires representations that are both fine-grained and broadly generalizable. This raises the following questions. How can the interactions of a given human-object pair, including interactions never observed during training, be recognized with such representations rather than through alignment with static text embeddings fitted to the seen categories, given that recognition is multi-label because one pair can be engaged in several interactions at once? Can interaction recognition be made independent of any particular object detector, so that it works with the boxes produced by any detector without retraining, stays reliable when those boxes are imperfect, and remains computationally tractable given the many human-object pairs and candidate interactions in an image?

Smoothed decision-making is critical to avoiding abrupt and potentially dangerous large changes of actions in many online optimization problems, such as energy production scheduling in power grids, object tracking, motion planning, and server capacity provisioning in data centers. Mathematically, action smoothness can be achieved by adding to the optimization objective a switching cost that penalizes temporal changes in actions. The switching cost equips the online objective with a (finite) memory of previous actions and creates substantial algorithmic challenges; smoothed online optimization has therefore received a great deal of attention over the last decade, with a quickly growing list of algorithms offering worst-case performance guarantees in adversarial and stochastic settings and under various extensions.

At the same time, long-term fairness is a crucial consideration in many online optimization problems that can profoundly affect individuals' well-being and social welfare. Sequential allocation of social goods to different individuals or groups must be fair and free of discrimination; the surging environmental costs of geographically distributed AI data centers must be fairly distributed across regions, as repeatedly called for by various organizations and government agencies; and AI model performance and resource provisioning must promote social fairness without adversely affecting disadvantaged individuals or groups. If not designed with fairness in mind, online algorithms can perpetuate or even exacerbate societal biases, disproportionately affect certain groups or individuals, and amplify already widening socioeconomic disparities. Fairness in online optimization is therefore not only an ethical concern but also a necessity for broader social responsibility.

Incorporating a long-term fairness regularizer into the objective can effectively promote fairness in online optimization by mitigating implicit or explicit biases, but it creates significant challenges. The regularizer depends on the entire trajectory of actions and contexts and can only be evaluated at the end of an episode, with complete information, whereas a switching cost can be assessed step by step. Online decision-makers react to sequentially revealed information and tend to prioritize immediate cost reduction, potentially neglecting the long-term consequences of their sequence of decisions.

Recent research has started to explore fairness and long-term constraints in online problems such as online resource allocation, using primal-dual techniques. A major limitation of current fair online algorithms, however, is their reliance on the assumption that per-round objective functions are independent of historical actions, an assumption that plays a pivotal role in both their algorithm design and their theoretical analysis. In a simple resource allocation problem, for instance, the maximum allowable action at a given time may depend on past decisions through the remaining budget, but the reward at that time is assumed to depend only on the current decision. Such methods fall short when the per-round objective is directly affected by previous irrevocable actions, as it is with switching costs; in that case an online algorithm and an offline benchmark face different per-round objectives because their action sequences differ, which complicates any direct comparison of their costs. Conversely, the rich literature on smoothed online optimization does not handle a regularizer that is evaluated over the whole horizon. Fairness-regularized smoothed online optimization with switching costs is thus a new and challenging setting that appears not to have been considered in the literature.

Formally, consider an episode of T rounds. At each round t, an agent observes a (potentially adversarially chosen) non-negative hitting cost function f_t and a matrix A_t that maps its action into an M-dimensional cost vector, each dimension corresponding to an entity for which fairness must be taken into account, and then chooses an irrevocable action x_t without knowing future information. It incurs the hitting cost f_t(x_t) and a switching cost d(x_t, x_{t-1}), for instance a scaled squared Euclidean distance between consecutive actions. Fairness is captured by a long-term cost g, convex and Lipschitz, applied to the episode average of the cost vectors; a well-known choice is an l_p norm, which prioritizes reducing the highest costs borne by disadvantaged entities and recovers min-max fairness as p tends to infinity. The goal is to minimize $\frac{1}{T}\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T} f_t(x_t) + \sum_{t=1}^{T} d(x_t, x_{t-1})\big) + g\big(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} A_t x_t\big)$.

This setting raises several questions. First, how hard is the long-term fairness regularizer intrinsically? Online algorithms are commonly evaluated by their regret or by their competitive ratio against a dynamic offline benchmark which, unlike a static benchmark restricted to a single fixed action, can adapt its action sequence over time with full knowledge of the context. A finite competitive ratio is attainable for online optimization with switching costs, but whether any online algorithm can achieve sublinear regret or a finite competitive ratio against the dynamic offline optimum in the presence of a long-term fairness regularizer, even without switching costs, remains an open question; prior work has only conjectured that finite performance might be impossible in similar settings. Second, if such guarantees are out of reach, against what kind of benchmark can meaningful, practically relevant performance guarantees be established? Third, how can an online algorithm reconcile the tension between minimizing the hitting cost, the switching cost and the long-term fairness cost with provable worst-case guarantees, when the per-round objective carries a memory of previous actions, and how does the long-term fairness regularizer affect such guarantees?

Geometry reconstruction is a fundamental problem that enables a wide range of applications in fields such as virtual reality and robotics. In recent years, neural reconstruction methods have gained significant attention; a key advantage of these methods is their ability to represent the geometry of a scene continuously, which can help in many downstream tasks. However, vision-based sensors often struggle in adverse weather conditions, or even become completely unusable when objects are obscured by occlusions.

Radio frequency (RF) sensing, specifically wireless millimeter-wave (mmWave) sensing, can see through occlusions, remains robust under challenging visibility conditions and, unlike X-rays, is not dangerous to humans, making it a compelling alternative for 3D reconstruction. This could open up many applications, for example checking whether the items inside a box are the correct items, are damaged, or pose a threat, without ever opening the box. On the other hand, mmWave resolution is extremely low compared to vision: a single radar image provides far less visual context than a camera image, which makes it hard to extract a 3D reconstruction from one radar image alone. Some prior RF systems have performed 3D point cloud reconstruction or human body tracking by leveraging movement or by emulating larger antenna apertures, but the recovered point clouds are still too sparse and noisy to reliably recover detailed geometry; through-wall human sensing relies on human motion to combat specularity, and deep learning on mmWave radar data has mostly targeted self-driving scenarios, where image resolution matters little. Other works have proposed neural implicit representations for RF sensing, aiming to concentrate scene information out of heavy noise through neural optimization, but these systems are designed for large-scale environments such as streets or satellite imagery and are far from achieving millimeter-level precision. When objects are close to the radar, the propagation characteristics of RF signals change dramatically: incoming waves can no longer be approximated as planar, so processing methods designed for large-scale scenes, such as beamforming, introduce a considerable amount of distortion and noise, often exceeding the noise acceptable for gradient descent and leading to unstable optimization. Existing neural RF reconstruction work is thus either limited to far-range scenes or, for individual objects, evaluated only on simulated data, which for wireless signals cannot come close to representing the complexity of real-world measurements. Meanwhile, the multi-view reconstruction and inverse rendering methods of computer vision (multi-view stereo, neural radiance fields, Gaussian splatting, neural implicit surfaces, physically based inverse rendering) are all derived from RGB images and are not easily transferable to mmWave data: even lensless RGB images can be mapped back to a lens-based imaging model without altering the underlying ray physics, whereas for RF signals such a transformation is fundamentally invalid.

The open problem is therefore to overcome the fundamental dilemma between massive RF noise in the input and the reconstruction of complete, high-resolution, millimeter-level 3D surface geometry of near-range objects, including objects hidden behind occlusions. This is not straightforward, because inferring surface geometry from RF signals differs fundamentally from image-based reconstruction in three main ways. First, wireless systems lack a lens-based imaging model: whereas lenses filter and focus the relevant light rays, radar antenna arrays perform lensless imaging and capture all incoming RF signals without directional filtering, which leads to low signal-to-noise ratios because irrelevant signals cannot be excluded. Second, RF signals and visible light propagate differently: visible light is predominantly scattered diffusely by surfaces, whereas RF signals, whose wavelengths are on the order of millimeters, are dominated by specular reflections, so volumetric rendering techniques designed for scattering-based vision sensors are unsuitable for RF imaging. Third, physically modeling lensless RF measurements is computationally expensive: whereas lens-based rendering samples along 1D rays, modeling what each antenna receives requires accounting for contributions from the full 3D space, leading to cubic complexity that makes naive implementations intractable at millimeter resolution.

How can accurate, millimeter-level 3D geometry of near-range objects be reconstructed from noisy real-world RF measurements, in line of sight and through occlusions, despite lensless imaging, specular reflections and the cost of modeling signal contributions from the full 3D space?
